questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why hippocampal damage spares old memories
questions.stem: Explain why damage to the hippocampus leaves a person able to recall childhood events but unable to form new lasting memories.

answer.exemplar: The hippocampus binds new experiences into durable long-term memories, but older memories are already stored across widespread cortex, so a damaged hippocampus blocks new consolidation while leaving old recollections intact.

questions.explanation: The hippocampus is needed to lay down new lasting memories, not to preserve the old ones that have already been consolidated.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain paired effects of opioid receptor activation
questions.stem: Explain why opioid drugs that occupy the same receptors can relieve pain and also slow breathing.

answer.exemplar: Opioid receptors sit both on pain-transmission pathways and on brainstem circuits that drive breathing, so a drug acting at those receptors dampens pain while simultaneously depressing respiratory drive, which is why the two effects appear together.

questions.explanation: Both effects trace to the same receptor family acting in different circuits, so pain relief and respiratory depression co-occur.
questions.hint: Where else are those receptors found?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: trace a transporter blockade on a diagram
questions.stem: A diagram shows a drug molecule docking on a presynaptic transporter and preventing transmitter pickup. What effect does that docking have?

options.text: Transmitter stays in the cleft longer
Transmitter release is blocked at the terminal
options.misconception: moves the block to release rather than cleanup

options.text: Vesicles stop forming in the cell body
options.misconception: shifts the effect to production

options.text: The receptor stops responding to all transmitters
options.misconception: overgeneralizes one specific dock

questions.explanation: Blocking the transporter stops reuptake, so the transmitter remains available in the synaptic cleft to act on receptors.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a claim about two drug mechanisms
questions.stem: A student claims that stimulating a receptor and blocking a transmitter's cleanup must produce opposite effects. What is the best evaluation?

options.text: False, both raise signaling by different routes
True, stimulation excites while blocking excites less
options.misconception: the second clause contradicts the first claim

options.text: False, both lower signaling in every case
options.misconception: denies the common direction of the effects

options.text: True, blocking cleanup only speeds the transmitter's loss
options.misconception: misstates what blocking cleanup does

questions.explanation: An agonist adds signal by activating receptors, while blocking cleanup adds signal by keeping transmitter present in the cleft.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: classify nicotine's action
questions.stem: Nicotine binds to receptors that normally receive acetylcholine. How should the drug's action be described?

options.misconception: flips mimicry into blockade
names a cleanup mechanism instead
names a breakdown pathway instead

questions.explanation: Nicotine occupies and activates acetylcholine receptors, so it behaves as an agonist at those sites.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: interpret tolerance and reversal data
questions.stem: Response to a fixed dose of a stimulant is measured across trials as 100, 80, 60, and then 95 after a drug-free break. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Tolerance builds during repeated dosing and partly reverses after the break
The drug's effect grows steadily with use
options.misconception: reverses the declining scores recorded

options.text: The break caused permanent loss of sensitivity
options.misconception: a later response recovered, so the loss is not permanent

options.text: Measurement error explains all of the change
options.misconception: dismisses a systematic, recoverable pattern

questions.explanation: A falling response to a fixed dose with partial recovery after abstinence is the classic tolerance and reversal pattern.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: match transmitter deficits to clinical patterns
questions.stem: Three patients show: one has low serotonin activity with persistent low mood, one has low acetylcholine with memory failure, and one has low dopamine with tremor. Which pairing is most defensible?

options.text: Low serotonin with mood, low acetylcholine with memory, low dopamine with movement
Low serotonin with tremor, low dopamine with memory
options.misconception: swaps two transmitter roles

options.text: Low acetylcholine with mood, low serotonin with movement
options.misconception: swaps the mood and memory roles

options.text: All three deficits share a single transmitter

questions.explanation: Serotonin is tied to mood regulation, acetylcholine to memory circuits, and dopamine to movement control.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain which drugs reach the brain
questions.stem: Explain why some drugs cross into the brain while other compounds cannot.

answer.exemplar: The brain is guarded by a blood-brain barrier of tightly joined vessel cells that only allows small and fat-soluble molecules through, so drugs designed to be lipid soluble reach brain tissue while large or water-loving compounds are turned away.

questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier filters by size and fat solubility, which decides whether a drug ever reaches brain receptors.
questions.hint: What kind of molecules get through the barrier?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: predict the symptoms of demyelination
questions.stem: A disease damages myelin in the central nervous system. What symptom pattern is most expected?

options.text: Loss of neurotransmitter receptors throughout the brain
options.misconception: blames receptor loss for an insulation defect

options.text: Complete inability to produce any action potential
options.misconception: the axon can still carry signals, just less well

options.text: Permanent loss of the resting potential
options.misconception: the resting potential persists despite the damage

questions.explanation: Demyelination slows and blocks conduction, producing weakness, numbness, and coordination problems rather than total signaling failure.
questions.hint: The axon is intact but the myelin is not.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: design a pain-blocking mechanism
questions.stem: A dentist wants a compound that stops tooth pain signals at the nerve without affecting muscle control. Draft the mechanism and predict one likely side effect.

answer.exemplar: Block voltage-gated sodium channels in the sensory nerve fibers so no action potential can be generated there, which stops the pain impulse before it reaches the brain; a likely side effect is numbness of the lip and tongue because those sensory fibers are blocked too.

questions.explanation: Blocking sodium channels stops the impulse in the nerve, so the pain signal never gets a route to the brain.
questions.hint: Which step of the impulse can be blocked?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a claim about regional specialization
questions.stem: A colleague argues that because the brainstem controls breathing, the cortex cannot affect emotions. What is the best evaluation?

options.text: The claim mixes levels; different regions handle different functions
The claim is correct because the brainstem is more ancient
options.misconception: confuses evolutionary age with functional exclusivity

options.text: The cortex controls breathing instead of the brainstem
options.misconception: reverses the known division of labor

options.text: Emotions are produced only by the spinal cord
options.misconception: places emotion outside the brain

questions.explanation: The brainstem does run autonomic functions, but cortical and limbic regions contribute separately to emotion, so both statements can be true at once.
